messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'Sync_Full_Bridge': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology b8c15461bdb9).
S1 S pzp out ctrl=G1
S2 S pzn 0 ctrl=G1
S3 S pzn out ctrl=G2
S4 S pzp 0 ctrl=G2
G1 SYNC ton=0.001s phase=0 edges=pos
G2 SYNC ton=0.001s phase=0 edges=neg
Cout C out 0 1e-05
Dz D 0 out DZ33
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: 18.8 uW of 21.6 uW needed (87 %); S4: -2.33 uW of 3.24 uW needed (-72 %); S6: 12.4 uW of 9.82 uW needed (126 %)
what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only 87 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -72 % of the load's need on S4 (weak excitation) (best of the value presets tried)

Design 2 'PSSHI_Fixed': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (c0001); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

[c0029] PSSHI_FBR_Zener  (topology 40eae91a637a, score 20.54, conditions passed 1/6)
L1 L pzp n1 0.01
S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
G1 SYNC ton=0.00023s phase=0.0615 edges=both
D1 D pzp out DSCH
D2 D pzn out DSCH
D3 D 0 pzp DSCH
D4 D 0 pzn DSCH
Dz D 0 out DZ33
Cout C out 0 2.83e-06
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.29    3.34     119   0.253      32.8  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S2       2.44    2.47    72.8   0.318      39.6  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S3        3.4    3.41    29.8   0.102      5.24  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S4       2.32     2.4     155   0.483       5.4  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       3.12    3.22     200    0.31      20.8  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S6       2.25    2.27    54.6   0.354      15.3  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       FAIL    
failing: S5 settled: 0.2124 V (needs <= 0.02 V, margin -9.62)
S4 settled: 0.1673 V (needs <= 0.02 V, margin -7.37)
S1 settled: 0.1622 V (needs <= 0.02 V, margin -7.11)

... and 3 more failing checks
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: 53.7 uW of 21.6 uW needed (249 %); S4: 30.8 uW of 3.24 uW needed (951 %); S6: 50 uW of 9.82 uW needed (509 %)
value sizing: 32/48 evaluations (running)
what this means:
- start-up is too slow on S4 (0.48 s): the storage charges too slowly from 0 V (too much capacitance or too little power at low voltage)
- the output is still drifting at 0.8 s on S1 (162 mV between windows), S2 (72 mV between windows), S4 (167 mV between windows) and 2 more: the storage time constant is too long
- ripple is too large on S1 (119 mV), S2 (73 mV), S4 (155 mV) and 2 more: the storage cannot buffer the charge pulses against the load

Topologies explored so far (hash: name, best score):

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor-node RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (settled mean)
    *   Piezo Model: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t) || C_p || 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Operating Conditions: S1-S6 (varying $I_p$, $f$, $C_p$, $R_L$).
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, 4 switches, 2 SYNC controllers.

    *   `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` ([c0029]) used an L-S (inductor-switch) loop for inversion and a full-bridge rectifier (FBR) with a zener clamp.
    *   Issues:
        *   $v_{pp}$ too large (ripple).
        *   $dv$ too large (not settled).
        *   $t_{up}$ too slow for S4.
    *   Analysis of `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` failures:
        *   The "not settled" and "ripple" issues strongly suggest that the storage capacitor $C_{out}$ is too small to buffer the energy pulses, *or* the tuning process is struggling to find the right $C_{out}$ because it's fighting against other constraints. Wait, looking at the "what this means" section: "the storage cannot buffer the charge pulses against the load" and "storage time constant is too long". These are contradictory. Usually, a larger $C_{out}$ reduces ripple but increases startup time.
        *   Let's re-read: "the output is still drifting... storage time constant is too long". This means $RC$ is too large. "ripple is too large... storage cannot buffer...". This means $C$ is too small.
        *   This conflict usually happens when the charging mechanism is inefficient or intermittent.

    *   The previous design used a "parallel" PSSHI (Parallel Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) approach: $L$ and $S$ were used to invert $C_p$ charge, and an FBR was used to rectify the piezo's AC output into the storage cap.
    *   Wait, the connectivity provided for `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` was:
        `L1 L pzp n1`
        `S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1`
        `D1 D pzp out DSCH`
        `D2 D pzn out DSCH`
        `D3 D 0 pzp DSCH`
        `D4 D 0 pzn DSCH`
        `Dz D 0 out DZ33`
        `Cout C out 0`
    *   Looking at this: the $L+S$ part is in parallel with the piezo ($pzp \to n1 \to pzn$). This is the standard PSSHI. The FBR is also in parallel.
    *   Problem: The FBR diodes (DSCH) have drops ($\sim 0.25\text{V}$). In a full bridge, the current passes through two diodes ($0.5\text{V}$ drop). The piezo open-circuit voltage is low ($3.2\text{V}$), so this drop is significant.
    *   More importantly, the FBR is always "on" when the piezo voltage exceeds $V_{out} + V_{diode}$. The PSSHI switch is designed to flip the voltage at the peak. If the FBR is there, it might be clamping the voltage or stealing current before the inversion can happen efficiently.

    *   Instead of a full bridge, we can use a synchronous rectifier or a half-wave rectifier with a charge pump, or simply optimize the PSSHI.
    *   A more efficient way to get energy out of a PSSHI circuit is to use a synchronous switch to transfer the charge.
    *   Alternative: SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) usually replaces the rectifier with a switch-based charge transfer.
    *   Let's try a "Standard SSHI" (not parallel). In SSHI, we use the inductor to flip the voltage of $C_p$, and we use a switch to move the charge to $C_{out}$.
    *   However, the rules allow `SYNC` and `S`. A common high-efficiency piezo circuit is the "SSHI" with a flipping inductor and a diode-capacitor rectifier (or a synchronous one).

    *   Let's try a simpler Synchronous Rectifier.
        *   Switch 1: `pzp` to `out` (closed when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$)
        *   Switch 2: `pzn` to `out` (closed when $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$)
        *   Wait, $V_{pzn}$ is negative when $V_{pzp}$ is positive.
        *   Let's try a PSSHI with a better output stage. Instead of FBR, maybe just two diodes? No, that's half-wave.
        *   What if we use a buck-boost or a charge pump? Too many components.

    *   Let's rethink the `PSSHI_FBR_Zener`. The failures were ripple and settling.
        Ripple $\propto \frac{I_{load}}{f C_{out}}$. To decrease ripple, $C_{out}$ must increase.
        Settling time $\tau \approx R_L C_{out}$. To decrease settling time, $C_{out}$ must decrease.
        This is the classic trade-off. If we can't satisfy both, we need a higher frequency of charging or a different way to buffer.
        Wait, the piezo frequency $f$ is $100\text{Hz}$. The ripple is from the $100\text{Hz}$ (or $200\text{Hz}$) charging pulses.
        If $C_{out}$ is $2.83\mu\text{F}$ and $R_L$ is $330\text{k}\Omega$, $\tau = 0.93\text{s}$.
        The simulation is $0.8\text{s}$. A time constant of $0.9\text{s}$ means the system will *never* settle in $0.8\text{s}$.
        To settle, we need $\tau < 0.1\text{s}$ (roughly). For $R_L = 330\text{k}\Omega$, $C_{out}$ should be around $300\text{nF}$.
        But if $C_{out} = 300\text{nF}$, the ripple $\Delta V \approx \frac{I_{load}}{f C_{out}} = \frac{1.8\text{V}/330\text{k}\Omega}{100\text{Hz} \cdot 300\text{nF}} \approx \frac{5.4\mu\text{A}}{30\mu\text{A}} = 0.18\text{V}$.
        This is $> 0.05\text{V}$.
        So we have a fundamental problem: $R_L$ is too large for the required ripple and settling time with a simple $C_{out}$ buffer at $100\text{Hz}$.

    *   *Wait!* Is there a way to increase the charging frequency?
        The PSSHI flips the voltage twice per period. That's $200\text{Hz}$.
        Is there a way to make the load "see" a different capacitor?
        No, but we can use a larger $C_{out}$ to kill the ripple and hope the "settled" check is more lenient, or find a way to charge it faster.
        Actually, if $C_{out}$ is too large, it won't reach $1.8\text{V}$ in $0.4\text{s}$ (startup failure).
        If $C_{out}$ is too small, it ripples too much.
        The "settled" check $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ is the killer.

    *   Let's look at the "settled" requirement again: `dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|`.
        This is the change in the *mean* value.
        If $V_{out}$ is approaching an asymptote, $dv$ will be small.
        The drift happens because the capacitor is charging slowly.
        If we can charge the capacitor faster (more power), it will reach the equilibrium faster.

    *   How to get more power?
        1. Reduce diode drops. (Use synchronous rectification).
        2. Improve the PSSHI inversion.
        3. Use a different topology.

    *   Let's try a Synchronous Rectifier (SR) instead of FBR.
        Instead of 4 diodes, we use 4 switches (or 2 switches if we are clever).
        With 2 SYNCs, we can have:
        SYNC1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (ton, edges="pos", phase=0)
        SYNC2: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (ton, edges="neg", phase=0)
        Wait, `pzn` is usually the ground for the piezo. If we connect `pzn` to `out`, we are shifting the ground.
        Correct SR for piezo:
        S1: `pzp` to `out`
        S2: `pzn` to `out`
        S3: `pzp` to `0`
        S4: `pzn` to `0`
        This is basically a full bridge. But we only have 2 SYNCs and 4 switches.
        Wait, the `SYNC` controller can handle "both" edges.
        Let's try:
        SYNC1: `ton`, edges="both", phase=0. (Close S1 and S3?)
        This is getting complicated.

    *   Let's try a different approach: A "Charge Pump" style PSSHI.
        Use the inductor to flip $C_p$, and a diode-capacitor network to step up the voltage.
        Actually, the simplest way to reduce the diode drop is to use only 2 diodes (half-wave) and an inductor, but that's less power.

    *   Let's consider the `Sync_Full_Bridge` (Design 1), which failed the screen.
        It tried to use switches as the bridge.
        S1: `pzp` $\to$ `out` (G1, pos)
        S2: `pzn` $\to$ `0` (G1, pos)
        S3: `pzn` $\to$ `out` (G2, neg)
        S4: `pzp` $\to$ `0` (G2, neg)
        This *is* a synchronous full bridge. Why did it fail the screen?
        Screen check: "out fixed at 1.8 V, net power delivered...".
        With $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$, the switch `pzp` $\to$ `out` only conducts if $V_{pzp} > 1.8\text{V}$.
        The piezo $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$.
        The issue might be the `ton` and `phase`. A synchronous bridge needs to be closed for a significant portion of the half-cycle, not just a short `ton` pulse.
        Wait, the `S` switch is closed for `ton` seconds. If `ton` is $0.001\text{s}$ (1ms) and the period is $10\text{ms}$, it's only on for 10% of the time.
        A rectifier should be on for ~50% of the time.
        BUT, the `S` switch is only for `ton`. `SYNC` is not a "comparator-based" switch; it's a "pulse-based" switch.
        This means we *cannot* use `S` as a standard rectifier. We can only use it for short bursts (like PSSHI inversion).
        For rectification, we *must* use diodes `D`.

    *   Okay, if we must use diodes for rectification, how to improve the FBR?
        The FBR has a $0.5\text{V}$ drop. For $V_{oc} = 3.2\text{V}$, that's $15\%$.
        We can use a "half-bridge" or a "charge pump" to reduce the drop.
        A Dickson charge pump? No, too many components.
        What about a "voltage doubler" (Greinacher circuit)?
        $C_1$ from `pzp` to `n1`
        $D_1$ from `n1` to `0`
        $D_2$ from `pzp` to `out`
        $C_2$ from `out` to `0`
        This is for AC sources. For piezo, it might work.

    *   Let's go back to `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` and try to fix the ripple/settling.
        The conflict is $C_{out}$ (large for ripple, small for settling).
        Is there any way to reduce the ripple without increasing $C_{out}$?
        Yes: increase the frequency of the charging pulses.
        The FBR already provides $200\text{Hz}$ pulses.
        What if we use a smaller $C_{out}$ and a *second* capacitor to filter the ripple?
        No, that doesn't make sense.
        Wait, if we use a larger $C_{out}$ and we want it to settle faster, we need to *charge* it faster.
        To charge it faster, we need more power.
        To get more power, we need to make the PSSHI more efficient.
        The `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` had $L=10\text{mH}$ and $ton=230\mu\text{s}$.
        Let's check $ton \approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p} = \pi\sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} = \pi\sqrt{250 \cdot 10^{-9}} = \pi \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-4} \approx 1.57\text{ms}$.
        The used `ton` was $0.23\text{ms}$. That's much shorter than $\pi\sqrt{LC_p}$.
        A shorter `ton` means the voltage is not fully flipped, which reduces the energy extracted per cycle.
        If we increase `ton`, we get more power $\to$ faster startup $\to$ faster settling.

    *   Wait, I can't change `ton` manually; the evolution strategy does that.
        But I can change the topology.
        What if I remove the FBR and use a more efficient synchronous transfer?
        Since `S` is only for short pulses, I can use `S` to transfer the charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ at the peak.
        Basically:
        1. Use $L+S_1$ to flip $C_p$ (PSSHI).
        2. Use $S_2$ to connect $C_p$ to $C_{out}$ at the peak.
        But $S_2$ would also only be on for `ton`. This is just a switched-capacitor converter.

    *   Let's try a "Half-Bridge" rectifier with a Zener clamp to see if it helps startup (lower diode drop).
        But FBR is generally better for power.

    *   Let's try a "Synchronous SSHI" (not parallel).
        In SSHI:
        Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Switch $\to$ Ground.
        This is too complex for the components allowed.

    *   Let's try to improve the `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` by adding a "pre-charge" or "startup" path? No.
        What if we use a different diode? `DSCH` is already the best.

    *   Let's try a topology called "Synchronous Charge Extraction" (SCE).
        S1: `pzp` to `out` (ctrl=G1, edges="pos", phase=0)
        S2: `pzn` to `out` (ctrl=G2, edges="neg", phase=0)
        As discussed, `S` is only on for `ton`.
        Wait, the rules say: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds".
        If I set `ton` to $1\text{ms}$, it's still small.
        But if I use a *large* inductor $L$ and a *small* $C_{out}$, I might get the ripple and settling right.

    *   Let's try a "Pseudo-Synchronous" bridge.
        Use the PSSHI to flip the voltage, but instead of FBR, use a simpler rectifier.
        Actually, let's try a "Half-Wave PSSHI" (just one diode to `out`).
        Wait, the reference FBR failed on S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation).
        S2 failure: $v_{avg} = 1.76\text{V}$ (needs $1.8\text{V}$).
        S4 failure: $v_{avg} = 1.51\text{V}$ (needs $1.8\text{V}$).
        This means FBR doesn't provide enough power.
        The `PSSHI_FBR_Zener` [c0029] *did* pass the $v_{avg}$ check for S2 and S4!
        S2: $v_{avg} = 2.44\text{V}$ (ok)
        S4: $v_{avg} = 2.32\text{V}$ (ok)
        So PSSHI + FBR *is* powerful enough. The only problems are ripple and settling.

    *   How to fix ripple and settling without changing the power?
        This is a capacitor sizing problem.
        If the evolution strategy couldn't find a $C_{out}$ that satisfies both, maybe the topology is limiting it.
        Wait, if $R_L$ is $330\text{k}\Omega$ and $C_{out}$ is $2.8\mu\text{F}$, the ripple is $\approx 20\text{mV}$ (which is ok), but the settling is $160\text{mV}$ (which is not ok).
        If we reduce $C_{out}$ to $1\mu\text{F}$, the ripple becomes $\approx 60\text{mV}$ (not ok), and the settling becomes $\approx 60\text{mV}$ (not ok).
        This means the "settled" check is very strict.
